title: HEROD ACCEPTED THE CROWD’S WORSHIP—THEN AN ANGEL STRUCK HIM
paragraphs: HEROD ACCEPTED THE CROWD’S WORSHIP—THEN AN ANGEL STRUCK HIM
The crowd called him a god. Herod did not correct them. Heaven did.
There are moments in Scripture that make you uncomfortable because they refuse to let you keep God small.
Acts 12 contains one of them.
A king sits before a crowd dressed in royal splendor. People are watching him. Listening to him. Depending upon him.
Then the shouting begins.
“Θεοῦ φωνὴ καὶ οὐκ ἀνθρώπου.”
Theou phōnē kai ouk anthrōpou.
“The voice of a god and not of a man.”
And Herod lets them say it.
That may be the most frightening part of the entire story.
He does not interrupt them.
He does not tear his garments.
He does not say, “No. I am only a man.”
He receives what belongs to God.
And then heaven answers.
Acts 12:23 records:
“Παραχρῆμα δὲ ἐπάταξεν αὐτὸν ἄγγελος Κυρίου ἀνθ’ ὧν οὐκ ἔδωκεν τὴν δόξαν τῷ Θεῷ…”
Parachrēma de epataxen auton angelos Kyriou… ouk edōken tēn doxan tō Theō…
In context, the meaning is devastatingly clear:
Immediately an angel of the Lord struck him because he did not give the glory to God.
Then Luke tells us that Herod became skōlēkobrōtos—“eaten by worms”—and breathed his last.
A man was being praised as divine one moment.
Then dying the next.
But before we point at Herod, perhaps we should ask the question this passage quietly forces upon every human heart:
What praise have I been accepting that should have passed through me and gone to God?
Because Herod’s temptation did not die with Herod.
It simply changed clothes.
We may never sit upon a royal throne.
Nobody may ever shout that we are gods.
But we know what it feels like to crave recognition.
To refresh the post.
To check the reactions.
To notice who complimented us.
To feel strangely disappointed when something we did received less attention than we thought it deserved.
We know how easily “God used me” can slowly become “look what I did.”
We know how subtly ministry can become identity.
How service can become performance.
How gifting can become entitlement.
How applause can become oxygen.
How even something done in Jesus’ name can quietly become something we need people to admire us for.
That is why Herod’s story is not merely ancient history.
It is a mirror.
And mirrors are uncomfortable when the lights are bright enough.
The surrounding context makes the scene even more sobering.
This is Herod Agrippa I, the ruler who had James the brother of John killed and had Peter arrested. Earlier in the same chapter, Peter is sitting in prison while believers are praying.
Herod has guards.
Peter has chains.
Herod has political authority.
The church has prayer.
Herod appears powerful.
The Christians appear helpless.
Then God moves.
An angel enters Peter’s prison.
Chains fall.
Doors open.
Peter walks out.
And later in the same chapter, another angel appears.
But this time the angel does not come to release a prisoner.
The angel comes in judgment against a king.
Do not miss the contrast.
The same chapter shows heaven opening prison doors for one man and bringing down another man who refuses to give God glory.
Human power looked enormous.
God was never intimidated.
And there is an extraordinary historical detail outside the New Testament that makes the scene even more striking.

The first-century Jewish historian Josephus independently describes the death of Agrippa at Caesarea. His account is not identical to Luke’s, and we should not force it to be. Josephus describes Agrippa appearing at a festival wearing a magnificent garment made of silver. Morning sunlight struck it, creating a dazzling spectacle. Flatterers began addressing him as a god.
Josephus says Agrippa did not rebuke them.
Then severe pain struck him, and he died after several days.
Luke gives us the theological reality behind Herod’s downfall: Herod failed to give glory to God.
Josephus supplies historical details from another perspective.
Different writers.
Different purposes.
Yet both preserve the haunting picture of a ruler receiving divine honors shortly before his death.
The applause did not save him.
The robe did not save him.
The throne did not save him.
His influence did not save him.
His title did not save him.
And there is something painfully modern about that.
We spend so much of our lives constructing robes.
Not literal silver garments.
Other kinds.
The successful marriage everybody sees.
The ministry everybody admires.
The career that proves we mattered.
The body we want people to notice.
The platform.
The followers.
The house.
The achievements.
The reputation.
Sometimes even the appearance of being spiritually strong.
We polish the outside until the light hits it just right.
And people applaud.
But God sees beneath the robe.
He sees the exhausted man secretly addicted to approval.
The woman comparing herself with everyone on her screen.
The pastor beginning to love the platform more than the presence of Christ.
The Christian who knows how to say “all glory to God” while secretly becoming angry when someone else receives the recognition.
The person who serves everyone but inwardly resents anyone who fails to notice.
The believer whose public Christianity looks alive while private prayer is almost gone.
And maybe that is where this story finds you.
Not on Herod’s throne.
But somewhere much quieter.
Maybe you have been starving for somebody to notice you.
Maybe rejection wounded you so deeply that admiration became medicine.
Maybe being overlooked made you promise yourself that one day everyone would see your worth.
Maybe you never wanted worship.
You just wanted to feel valuable.
And somewhere along the way, human approval became the place you started looking for what only God could give you.
This is where the Gospel changes the entire story.
Because Christianity does not merely tell you, “Stop being proud.”
Christianity gives you Someone infinitely greater than your pride.
Jesus Christ.
Think about the contrast.
Herod receives glory that does not belong to him.
Jesus possesses glory that actually does belong to Him.
Yet Christ humbled Himself.
Herod sits dressed as royalty while people exalt him.
Jesus, the true King, is stripped and mocked.
Herod receives the cry of people treating him like a god.
Jesus is God the Son, yet He allows sinful men to ridicule Him.
Herod clings to glory.
Jesus walks toward a cross.
Herod wants elevation.
Jesus embraces humiliation for sinners.
And at Calvary, the King who deserved every angelic song willingly endured human mockery so rebels like us could receive mercy.
This is why the answer to pride is not merely trying harder to think less of yourself.
The answer is seeing Christ more clearly.
When you see Him…
His holiness makes your self-exaltation ridiculous.
His cross makes your self-righteousness impossible.
His grace makes hiding unnecessary.
His resurrection makes earthly applause temporary.
His love makes the approval of crowds insufficient.
And His glory makes surrender beautiful.
The Gospel says you do not have to manufacture your significance.
You do not have to become your own god.
You do not have to convince everyone that you matter.
At the cross, Jesus Christ demonstrates both the horror of sin and the staggering depth of divine mercy.
The One who deserved glory took shame.
The guilty can receive grace.
The proud can repent.
The hidden can come into the light.
The spiritually exhausted can stop performing.
The sinner can come home.
That is From Scandal to Grace.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
But Acts does something brilliant after Herod dies.
Luke does not end the scene with worms.
He writes:
Ho de logos tou theou ēuxanen kai eplēthyneto.
“But the word of God continued to grow and multiply.”
Herod dies.
The Word keeps moving.
Read that again.
Herod dies.
The Word keeps moving.
Kings disappear.
The Word remains.
Empires collapse.
The Word remains.
Celebrities are forgotten.
The Word remains.
Platforms vanish.
The Word remains.
Algorithms change.
The Word remains.
Your name and mine will eventually disappear from human conversation.
Jesus Christ will still be King.
Perhaps freedom begins when that stops frightening us.
You do not need your name to last forever.
You need His Name to be glorified through the life you have been given.
John the Baptist understood it:
“He must increase, but I must decrease.”
That is not self-hatred.
That is freedom.
Freedom from having to be impressive.
Freedom from having to win every argument.
Freedom from needing everybody to recognize your sacrifice.
Freedom from pretending you are stronger than you are.
Freedom from building a throne inside your heart and begging people to sit beneath it.
And maybe right now the Holy Spirit is touching something you would rather keep hidden.
That craving for validation.
That jealousy.
That secret resentment.
That hunger to be seen.
That habit of comparing yourself.
That spiritual performance.
That quiet pride nobody around you knows exists.
Do not run from conviction.
Run to Jesus.
Conviction that drives you toward Christ is mercy.
Repentance is not God humiliating you for pleasure. Biblical repentance is turning from sin and returning to the God whose grace is greater than the identity you built without Him.
Tell Him the truth.
“Jesus, I have wanted glory that belongs to You.”
“Jesus, I have cared too much about what people think.”
“Jesus, forgive my pride.”
“Jesus, tear down every throne I have built for myself.”
“Jesus, teach me to live so people see You instead of me.”
And remember: we are not saved because we become humble enough.
We are saved by grace through faith in Jesus Christ.
The same Gospel that exposes our pride offers forgiveness to the proud.
The cross says your sin is serious.
The cross also says mercy is available.
Christ died for sinners.
Christ rose again.
And the King who humbled Himself will one day be openly acknowledged as Lord.
So come down from the little throne before which you have been exhausting yourself.
You were never created to carry the weight of being your own god.
Let Jesus be King.
And if this exposed something hidden in you, do not hide behind a polished Christian answer.
Not because typing words saves anyone.
Jesus saves.
But sometimes confession begins when we finally stop pretending the battle is not there.

And if you are still fighting the need for approval, comment, “I’m still fighting.” Let another believer reading these words realize they are not the only person learning to surrender their pride to Christ.

Your support helps us keep creating and sharing Scripture-centered content that calls people toward Jesus, repentance, grace, forgiveness, redemption, and transformed lives. And sharing these articles costs nothing while helping biblical truth reach people who might never walk into a church but will stop for a story appearing in their feed.
And do not keep the invitation to yourself.
Invite your family.
Invite the friend drifting from God.
Invite the believer who is exhausted.
Invite the person who has questions about Jesus.
Invite even the person who does not yet believe.
But whatever you do after reading this, remember the lesson of Acts 12.
Do not confuse applause with approval from God.
Do not confuse visibility with spiritual authority.
Do not confuse influence with holiness.
Do not mistake a shining robe for a surrendered heart.
Herod had a throne.
He had an audience.
He had authority.
He had applause.
For one terrifying moment, people even called him divine.
And none of it could give him another breath when God required an account.
Yet the chapter does not ultimately leave us staring at a dead king.
It leaves us staring at a living Word that keeps multiplying.
That is the choice hidden inside this story.
Build your life around a name that will disappear…
or surrender your life to the Name above every name.
Jesus does not need another competitor for His throne.
He is calling sinners to come down from theirs.
And perhaps the greatest thing that could happen to your reputation is that people eventually forget how impressive you were—but never forget the Jesus they saw changing you.
The crowd can give you a throne for a moment. Only Jesus can give you grace that survives the grave.
